The Cambridge Dictionary’s “word of the year” — parasocial — doesn’t merely stand in for
the one-sided bonds forged with celebrities, “content” creators and influencers through their
social-media presence. It captures the strange comfort of relationships in which reciprocity is
optional and intimacy outsourced; where the emotional upheavals in the lives of distant stars
— engagements, breakups, marriages, burnouts — feel more relatable than the well-meaning
neighbour one keeps stonewalling in the elevator.


In the early 1950s when television started becoming a fixture in middle-class homes, University
of Chicago sociologists Donald Horton and Richard Wohl observed a curious phenomenon —
viewers had begun forming attachments with stars and sportsmen that mimicked real life. They
named the phenomenon “parasocial”. As pop star Taylor Swift’s engagement news sent
followers into a frenzy, as listeners found their own heartbreaks reflected in Lily Allen’s
breakup album West End Girl, the coinage became a shorthand for a cultural reality in which
the emotional lives of famous strangers began to feel intimately like one’s own. In this, the
perpetually online may lead the charge, but the terrain they occupy is common ground.


What this says about the modern condition, though, is harder to dismiss: In a hyper-connected
world, loneliness has found subtler ways to settle in. It manifests itself in weightless
relationships with AI companions and chatbots, in the endless scroll through curated lives, in
the inability to reach out and forge IRL relationships with all their vulnerabilities. But that has
always been the challenge: To follow the spark, to hold on and to hang in when nothing makes
sense, until it does.

She may be only four months old and more than a few feathers short in one wing, but when
Frankie the flamingo heard the call of the wild, she responded in the only way she could — by
trusting her instincts and winging it. The juvenile bird, whose disappearance from her home at
a zoo in the UK last week prompted a nationwide search, has been found happy and thriving
on a beach in France’s Brittany region. Among the staff at Cornwall’s Paradise Park, who
identified their missing bird by the clipped wing visible in pictures taken by a French
photographer, her discovery evinced mixed emotions: Relief that she’s safe, worry about her
future and pride at her resilience.


That Frankie did not allow a literally clipped wing to ground her and curb her yearning for
freedom should be an inspiration for all, not least for the chronic overthinkers who rein in their
dreams and make peace with what they believe to be their lot. Frankie let nothing stand in her
way: Not her relative youth, not the missing portion of her wing and certainly not the fact that,
having been born and bred in a zoo, she’s never had to deal with the harshness that all living
things have to endure in the wild.


Frankie is thriving in the world beyond her enclosure. She can’t go home again, given the
possibility of her exposure to wild avian populations that may be infected with bird flu, but that
is a regret that the zoo, and the people who once watched over her, can nurse. Frankie the
flamingo is too busy being just another bird: Eating, preening and existing on no one’s terms
but her own.

As much as the Epstein saga seems like a bottomless cesspit, its central disjuncture is how
many of America’s rich and powerful, have been spotted swimming in it. Such disjunctures are
comedy gold, but only if the comic has empathy and moral muscle, besides wit and intelligence.
Lesser pens can trivialise the horrific abuse of children for TRPs. Finer ones can make a
difficult topic accessible to people, even as they demand political accountability. While usually
docile Republicans push Trump to cede ground on the release of the Epstein files, late night
US TV has kept up its job of landing endless punches. These make clear how, despite recent
setbacks, comedy still remains in better humour in this country than others.


A lot of it is decidedly non-snobby. On The Daily Show, Josh Johnson described Republicans
releasing 23,000 pages of Epstein documents to counter the three emails released by Democrats
as “trying to hide pissing yourself by shitting yourself”. And Jon Stewart talked about how
near-impossible it is to talk about this saga without sounding “ejaculate-adjacent”. The verb
‘release’ being Exhibit A. There is an air of ‘vox populi’ about all this. It’s in the hoary tradition
of jesters and wise fools. Another aspect of it is, as Shakespeare wrote in Twelfth Night, “What
great ones do, the less will prattle of.” But great and less have to be understood as inverse as
well. The Epstein files don’t just implicate Trump and Bill Clinton. Peter Thiel, Noam
Chomsky, Larry Summers, Steve Bannon – the Who’s Who featured here are from across the
political, financial, academic aisles. When the moral squalor is in high places, political humour
enables people to criticise it, whether or not the powerful are finally punished for it.


If the Epstein story has shown how humour keeps public attention focused on injustice in
America, in India too standup is having a golden moment. Bihar elections, for example, put the
spotlight on how many young people from the state are dishing out social-political laughter to
packed clubs, from Gurgaon to Bengaluru. This is a new kind of ‘adda’ space – serving
conscience plus chuckles. But whereas the worst that US comics have to fear is getting
cancelled, here there’s the whole gamut of FIRs, arrests, physical attacks to be dreaded. This
is very uncool. Comedy often turns sharper as the stakes go higher. It shouldn’t take uncommon
courage to tell a stinging joke.

questions.stimulus:
The death sentence given to former Bangladesh premier Sheikh Hasina by a domestic war
crimes court for ordering the use of lethal force against student-led protests that led to the ouster
of her government last year is unlikely to reduce the political instability in the country. Hasina,
who has been in self-exile in India since she left Bangladesh in August 2024, and her former
home minister were tried in absentia by the International Crimes Tribunal set up by the current
regime and both sentenced to death for their complicity in the death of protesters during the
tumultuous movement that rocked the country for weeks. The tribunal cited Hasina’s remarks
in recent interviews to the Indian media, acknowledging “supreme command responsibilities”
for the handling of the protests, as proof of her complicity in the killings. According to a United
Nations report, 1,400 people were killed during the protests.


The verdicts, in a way, reflect the vendetta politics that have long harmed India’s
neighbourhood. In the past, Hasina’s Awami League and its main opponent, the Bangladesh
Nationalist Party, resorted to similar measures against each other whenever they were in power.
Recent events, including two nationwide lockdowns called by the Awami League since last
week, have shown that it remains a political force in Bangladesh, though its capabilities may
have been diminished. The caretaker government led by Muhammad Yunus's decision to ban
the Awami League's activities certainly does not
well for its promise to hold free and fair elections. It is in this context that the Indian side has
maintained that Bangladesh’s general election, scheduled for February, must be free, fair and
inclusive.


                                     12minutestoclat.com                                          10


Following Hasina’s conviction and sentencing, Bangladesh’s interim government has doubled
down on its demand for the extradition of the former premier — a request that New Delhi has
not acted upon since it was received late last year. This will further strain India-Bangladesh
relations, which have been in decline since the Yunus-led regime assumed office. For the
Indian side, any further chaos and instability in Bangladesh has the potential to affect the
security and economic progress of the country’s sensitive northeastern states, which have
already been affected by the curtailment of connectivity and trade ties with Dhaka. India will
do well to prepare for what is likely to be another disruptive spell in relations with Bangladesh.

questions.stimulus:
LEGAL REASONING

Section 74 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, governs compensation for breach of contract
where the parties have stipulated a sum payable upon breach, or where the contract contains a
penalty clause. The provision creates a single, unified remedy: the party who suffers the breach
is entitled to receive "reasonable compensation" not exceeding the stipulated sum, regardless
of whether actual damage is proved. The classic judicial interpretation of this section required
courts to ask whether the stipulated sum was a "genuine pre-estimate" of loss anticipated at the
time of contracting. Where the sum was disproportionate to any conceivable injury, courts
treated it as a penalty and awarded only proved damages.

However, this approach drew criticism for its rigidity, particularly in commercial contracts
where sophisticated parties negotiate penalty clauses as instruments of risk allocation rather


                                   12minutestoclat.com                                       21


than mere damage estimates. English law had already moved away from the genuine pre-
estimate test in Cavendish Square Holdings v. Makdessi (2015), adopting instead a "legitimate
business interest" inquiry: a stipulated sum is enforceable if it is not extravagant or
unconscionable compared to the legitimate business interest it protects.

The Supreme Court of India, in BPL Ltd. v. Morgan Securities (2026), endorsed a similar
evolution. The Court held that where both parties are commercial entities with equal bargaining
power, a liquidated damages clause should be tested not against whether it was a genuine pre-
estimate, but whether the promisee had a legitimate business interest in enforcing performance,
and whether the stipulated sum was proportionate to that interest. The Court clarified that
Section 74 does not abolish penalty clauses altogether; rather, it subjects them to a
proportionality-and-legitimacy review. A clause that protects a real commercial interest, even
if it exceeds actual loss, may be enforceable if it satisfies this test. The Court further cautioned
that courts must not rewrite commercial bargains struck at arm's length between informed
parties.

questions.stimulus:
The Constitution (Scheduled Castes) Order, 1950, issued by the President of India under Article
341 of the Constitution, defines which communities are recognised as Scheduled Castes for
constitutional purposes. Paragraph 3 of that Order, as amended in 1956, provides that no person
professing a religion other than Hinduism, Sikhism, or Buddhism shall be deemed a member
of a Scheduled Caste. The practical effect of this provision is significant: a person born into a
Scheduled Caste who converts to Christianity or Islam loses the constitutionally recognised SC
status for the purposes of all legal benefits, reservations, and protections that flow from that
classification.

This has direct consequences under the SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989, which
creates special offences and enhanced penalties for crimes committed against persons
belonging to Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes. The Act's protections are triggered by
the victim's status as a member of an SC or ST community. Where the victim has converted to


                                    12minutestoclat.com                                       24


a religion outside the three recognised faiths under the 1950 Order, they no longer hold SC
status in the eyes of the law, and the Act accordingly ceases to apply to offences against them.

Courts have consistently applied this framework without extending its protections by analogy.
The rationale advanced for limiting SC status to Hinduism, Sikhism, and Buddhism is that the
caste system, as a social institution rooted in hierarchical religious practice, is historically
linked to these faiths. Whether a convert continues to face social discrimination has been
treated as a separate question from whether the legal definition of SC status is satisfied. The
1950 Order has been affirmed by the Supreme Court as a valid exercise of the power conferred
by Article 341, and Parliament alone has the competence to amend it.

       formally reconverts to Hinduism. He is then denied promotion in government service
       on grounds the state claims are caste-based. He invokes the SC/ST Act. Under the legal
       framework described, which outcome is most consistent?

options.label: a
options.text:
Rajan is entitled to SC status upon reconversion to Hinduism, making him eligible for
       the Act's protections if the denial was caste-motivated.

options.label: b
options.text:
Rajan cannot reclaim SC status since any prior conversion permanently disqualifies him
       under Paragraph 3, regardless of subsequent reconversion.

options.label: c
options.text:
The Act applies to Rajan irrespective of religion since the denial was motivated by his
       birth caste, which courts recognise as the operative criterion.


                                   12minutestoclat.com                                       25

options.label: d
options.text:
Rajan retains SC status throughout because conversions between Hindu denominations
      and Christianity are treated as intra-faith transitions under Article 341.

questions.stimulus:
The Constitution (Scheduled Castes) Order, 1950, issued by the President of India under Article
341 of the Constitution, defines which communities are recognised as Scheduled Castes for
constitutional purposes. Paragraph 3 of that Order, as amended in 1956, provides that no person
professing a religion other than Hinduism, Sikhism, or Buddhism shall be deemed a member
of a Scheduled Caste. The practical effect of this provision is significant: a person born into a
Scheduled Caste who converts to Christianity or Islam loses the constitutionally recognised SC
status for the purposes of all legal benefits, reservations, and protections that flow from that
classification.

This has direct consequences under the SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989, which
creates special offences and enhanced penalties for crimes committed against persons
belonging to Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes. The Act's protections are triggered by
the victim's status as a member of an SC or ST community. Where the victim has converted to


                                    12minutestoclat.com                                       24


a religion outside the three recognised faiths under the 1950 Order, they no longer hold SC
status in the eyes of the law, and the Act accordingly ceases to apply to offences against them.

Courts have consistently applied this framework without extending its protections by analogy.
The rationale advanced for limiting SC status to Hinduism, Sikhism, and Buddhism is that the
caste system, as a social institution rooted in hierarchical religious practice, is historically
linked to these faiths. Whether a convert continues to face social discrimination has been
treated as a separate question from whether the legal definition of SC status is satisfied. The
1950 Order has been affirmed by the Supreme Court as a valid exercise of the power conferred
by Article 341, and Parliament alone has the competence to amend it.

      her a reserved-category promotion and she claims the SC/ST Act's protection. The court
      should hold:

options.label: a

Kavitha loses SC status on conversion to Buddhism since caste-based social hierarchy
      is not recognised within Buddhist doctrine, disqualifying her from Article 341 benefits.

options.label: b
options.text:
Kavitha's claim fails because the SC/ST Act does not apply to workplace disputes
      involving reservations in service matters under private employment.

options.label: c
options.text:
Kavitha retains SC status because Buddhism is one of the three recognised faiths under
      the 1950 Order, and Paragraph 3 does not exclude Buddhist converts.

options.label: d
options.text:
Kavitha's claim is governed exclusively by the Persons with Disabilities Act and not
      the SC/ST Act once she leaves Hindu personal law by converting.

questions.stem:
Parliament proposes to amend the Constitution (Scheduled Castes) Order, 1950, to
      extend SC recognition to Christian and Muslim converts from SC communities. A
      petitioner challenges Parliament's competence to do so. Under the framework set out,

Parliament lacks competence since the 1950 Order was issued by presidential authority
      under Article 341 and is insulated from legislative amendment.

options.label: b

Parliament alone has the authority to amend the 1950 Order, as Article 341 explicitly

Farida, born into a Scheduled Caste community, converted to Christianity twenty years
      ago. She is attacked by a group motivated by her original caste identity. She argues she
      continues to experience caste discrimination despite her conversion. Her counsel

      Under the legal position described, the court should:

questions.stimulus:
The Special Marriage Act, 1954, provides a secular mechanism for civil marriage in India,
enabling persons of any religion, caste, or nationality to solemnise and register their union
outside the framework of personal religious laws. The Act prescribes minimum age
requirements of twenty-one years for the male party and eighteen years for the female party at
the time of marriage.

The procedure under the Act requires the parties to give a notice of intended marriage to the
Marriage Officer of the district where either party has resided for at least thirty days before the
notice. This notice is entered in a public register and is open to inspection by any person without
payment of a fee, creating a transparency mechanism that has drawn criticism for potentially
endangering couples whose families oppose the union. Within thirty days of the notice, any
person may object to the marriage on limited grounds: namely, that the marriage would
contravene any condition specified in the Act. These conditions include age requirements,
prohibited degrees of relationship, an existing subsisting marriage of either party, and the
mental incapacity of either party. The Marriage Officer must inquire into every objection and
may refuse registration only if the objection falls within these enumerated grounds.

Once the marriage is solemnised and the Marriage Officer issues a certificate, that certificate
serves as conclusive proof of the marriage. The certificate is not merely evidence of
solemnisation; it establishes the fact of marriage with finality for all legal purposes.

An important consequence concerns succession: where a marriage is registered under the
Special Marriage Act, the succession to the parties' property, and to the property of their
children, is governed by the Indian Succession Act, 1925, irrespective of the personal law that


                                    12minutestoclat.com                                         27


would otherwise apply to either party. This means that a Hindu who marries under the Special
Marriage Act is not governed by the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, in matters of inheritance.
questions.stem:

       register their marriage under the Special Marriage Act. Preethi's family objects, arguing
       the marriage would cause social harm and the couple lacks maturity. The Marriage
       Officer should:

options.label: a
options.text:
Defer solemnisation for six months to allow both families an opportunity to present
       their objections formally through a court of competent jurisdiction.

options.label: b
options.text:
Accept the objection since the Act permits any person to object on grounds that the
       marriage is contrary to the interests of the female party.

options.label: c
options.text:
Reject the objection, since the grounds of social harm and immaturity are not among
       the statutory grounds for objection, but must also refuse registration because Arjun is
       below twenty-one.

options.label: d
options.text:
Proceed with solemnisation since both parties satisfy the minimum age requirements
       and no valid statutory ground for objection has been raised.

questions.stem:
Rehana, a Muslim woman, marries Suresh, a Hindu man, under the Special Marriage
       Act. Suresh dies intestate. Rehana claims succession under Muslim personal law,
       arguing that her religion governs her inheritance rights. Under the Act's framework, the

questions.stem:
Nadia, born into a Hindu family, marries Kunal under the Special Marriage Act. They
      have a son, Rohit. Nadia dies without a will. Her mother claims a share of Nadia's estate
      under the Hindu Succession Act, 1956. Rohit claims the Indian Succession Act, 1925,
      applies and excludes his grandmother from inheriting. Under the applicable law:

options.text:
Hindu Succession Act governs since Nadia's religion was Hindu at death, and a civil
      marriage registration does not alter personal law governing inheritance.

options.label: b
options.text:
Indian Succession Act, 1925, governs succession to Nadia's estate, which may alter the
      shares available to her mother compared to Hindu Succession Act rules.

options.label: c

Rohit and Nadia's mother take equal shares under the Indian Succession Act, since
      intestate succession under that Act places children and parents on the same footing.

options.label: d

The marriage registration has no effect on succession law governing Nadia's estate; her
      pre-marital religious personal law continues to govern her intestate succession.

questions.stimulus:
The growth of platform-based gig work in India prompted legislative action at both the central
and state levels. The Social Security Code, 2020, for the first time recognised "gig workers"
and "platform workers" as distinct categories in Indian labour law. The Code mandates that the
central government formulate welfare schemes for such workers covering life and disability
cover, health and maternity benefits, old age protection, and other benefits. The Code also
obligates aggregators, defined as digital intermediaries connecting buyers and service
providers, to contribute to a social security fund at a rate between one and two percent of their
annual turnover, as notified by the government.

Building on the central framework, the Karnataka Platform Based Gig Workers (Social
Security and Welfare) Act, 2025, introduced several distinct mechanisms. The Act establishes
a dedicated social security fund for gig workers in Karnataka. Aggregators operating in
Karnataka are required to pay a mandatory welfare fee on every transaction: the fee is capped
at one and a half percent of the transaction payout made to the gig worker, rather than being
calculated on overall turnover. This distinction is operationally significant. The Act also
imposes transparency obligations, requiring aggregators to disclose the basis of algorithmic
assignment of work, deactivation criteria, and earnings computations to workers and to a
designated state authority.

A grievance mechanism under the Karnataka Act entitles gig workers to seek redressal before
a board, with a time-bound response obligation on aggregators. Importantly, the Act contains
a set-off provision: contributions made by aggregators under the central Social Security Code
towards gig worker welfare may be set off against the welfare fee payable under the Karnataka
Act, preventing double payment for the same benefit period. This set-off operates automatically
upon verified submission of proof of central contributions to the Karnataka welfare board.
questions.stem:
Quickride, a ride-hailing aggregator, operates in Karnataka and contributes one percent
       of its annual turnover to the central social security fund as required under the Social
       Security Code, 2020. In the same financial year, Karnataka's welfare board demands


                                   12minutestoclat.com                                        30


      the mandatory welfare fee under the 2025 Act. Quickride argues for a set-off. Under
      the framework described, which outcome is most consistent?

options.label: a
options.text:
Quickride may set off its verified central contributions against the Karnataka welfare
      fee, provided it submits proof of central contributions to the Karnataka board.

options.label: b
options.text:
Quickride must pay the Karnataka welfare fee in full, since state obligations are legally
      distinct from central contributions and no set-off is permitted between them.

options.label: c
options.text:
The set-off applies automatically without any submission requirement, since the 2025
      Act provides for self-executing relief upon the aggregator meeting the central
      obligation.

options.label: d
options.text:
Quickride is exempt from the Karnataka welfare fee entirely because it has already
      discharged its obligations to gig workers through the central scheme.

questions.stem:
DeliverFast, an aggregator, calculates its welfare fee under the Karnataka Act by
      applying one and a half percent to its gross platform revenue in Karnataka, not to the
      amounts paid out to individual gig workers. A gig worker union challenges this
      computation. Under the Act's mechanism as described, the challenge is:

options.text:
Unsustainable, since aggregators retain discretion to apply the welfare fee percentage
      to the base they consider most operationally practical given their accounting structure.

options.label: b
options.text:
Unsustainable, since the Karnataka Act's welfare fee and the central Code's turnover-
      based contribution are interchangeable, permitting either base for calculation.

Sustainable only in part, since the Act permits aggregators to choose between gross
      revenue and transaction payout as the fee base, subject to state authority approval.

      gig worker, not on the aggregator's overall revenue or platform turnover.

questions.stimulus:
In public employment governed by reservation policies, a recurring legal question concerns
whether a candidate from a reserved category who performs sufficiently well may be
considered for appointment against an unreserved or "open category" post, a process commonly
described as "migration." Migration occurs when a reserved category candidate's performance,
evaluated entirely on merit, places them above the last unreserved candidate in the open merit
list. In such cases, the candidate is appointed against the open category seat and the reserved
category vacancy remains available for other eligible candidates, thus enlarging the total
benefit to reserved category communities.

A distinct question arises where recruitment rules provide relaxations to reserved category
candidates at the eligibility stage. For instance, qualifying examinations such as the Teacher
Eligibility Test (TET) may prescribe a lower minimum passing threshold for SC/ST/OBC
candidates than for general category candidates. Candidates who clear the examination at the
relaxed threshold are fully eligible to participate in recruitment. The legal dispute is whether
having availed such a relaxation in qualifying marks bars a candidate from subsequently
migrating to the open category if their final selection score exceeds general category
candidates.

The Supreme Court addressed this question in Chaya v. State of Maharashtra (2026). The Court
held that a relaxation in qualifying marks affects eligibility alone, not a candidate's merit as
assessed in the main selection process. Once a candidate clears the qualifying examination,
their merit is determined independently and solely through the selection process. Accordingly,
having used a relaxed qualifying threshold does not bar migration to the open category unless
the applicable recruitment rules expressly prohibit it. In the absence of such a prohibition,
migration remains available to any reserved category candidate whose merit in the selection
process places them ahead of the last general category candidate appointed.

The Transfer of Property Act, 1882, recognises several forms of mortgage, each carrying
distinct legal characteristics and enforcement mechanisms. In a simple mortgage, the
mortgagor does not deliver possession of the property but personally covenants to repay the
debt and agrees that upon default the mortgagee may cause the property to be sold. A
usufructuary mortgage transfers possession of the mortgaged property to the mortgagee,
entitling the mortgagee to receive the rents and profits until the debt is discharged; no personal
decree for the mortgage money lies under this form. A mortgage by deposit of title deeds, also
called an equitable mortgage, arises in certain specified cities where a debtor delivers
documents of title to a creditor with the intent of creating a security interest; no registration is
required for this form.

Enforcement of a mortgage typically proceeds through a suit for foreclosure, sale, or
redemption before a civil court. Courts exercising equitable jurisdiction retain inherent
authority to mould relief in mortgage matters, balancing the creditor's right to recover against
the hardship faced by the mortgagor. Statutory provisions and judicial practice recognise One
Time Settlement (OTS) schemes offered by banks and financial institutions, which allow
borrowers to settle outstanding mortgage dues at a negotiated figure, often below the book
value of the debt.

In Sumaiya Parveen v. Central Bank of India (2026), the Supreme Court was confronted with
a situation where a widow sought to avail an OTS scheme offered by the bank, but the offer
had lapsed before she could complete payment due to circumstances beyond her control. The
bank refused to extend the scheme. The Supreme Court, invoking its plenary power under
Article 142 of the Constitution to do complete justice, directed the bank to honour the OTS
arrangement on the original terms. The Court characterised its intervention as an exercise of
equitable jurisdiction available in exceptional circumstances to prevent manifest injustice.

entitling the mortgagee to receive the rents and profits until the debt is discharged; no personal

documents of title to a creditor with the intent of creating a security interest; no registration is
required for this form.

redemption before a civil court. Courts exercising equitable jurisdiction retain inherent
authority to mould relief in mortgage matters, balancing the creditor's right to recover against
the hardship faced by the mortgagor. Statutory provisions and judicial practice recognise One
Time Settlement (OTS) schemes offered by banks and financial institutions, which allow
borrowers to settle outstanding mortgage dues at a negotiated figure, often below the book
value of the debt.

a situation where a widow sought to avail an OTS scheme offered by the bank, but the offer
had lapsed before she could complete payment due to circumstances beyond her control. The
bank refused to extend the scheme. The Supreme Court, invoking its plenary power under
Article 142 of the Constitution to do complete justice, directed the bank to honour the OTS

questions.stimulus:
Most people in the world eat meat, yet very few have visited a factory farm. This gap between
consumption and knowledge matters, because the conditions in industrial animal agriculture
are far removed from the pastoral images that appear on food packaging. The vast majority of
chickens, pigs, and cattle raised for food in the world today are kept in concentrated animal
feeding operations, commonly known as CAFOs. In these facilities, animals are often confined
in spaces so small that they cannot turn around, engage in natural behaviours, or avoid contact
with their own waste.
The scale of this system is staggering. Roughly 80 billion land animals are slaughtered for food
each year globally. Scientists and veterinarians broadly agree that pigs, cows, and chickens are
sentient creatures capable of experiencing pain, stress, and fear. When animals raised in
CAFOs exhibit behaviours such as feather-pecking, tail-biting, and repetitive pacing, these are
widely understood by animal behaviourists as signs of chronic stress caused by confinement
and deprivation of natural stimuli.
Defenders of industrial farming argue that it is the only way to produce enough food at prices
ordinary people can afford. They point out that modern food systems have made protein
accessible to populations that once faced serious nutritional deficits, and that improving
conditions for farm animals would inevitably raise costs and price poorer consumers out of the
market. Some also argue that because humans are omnivores by nature, there is nothing
inherently wrong with using animals for food.
Critics of this view respond that the argument from necessity is weaker than it appears. Food
systems could be reorganised to produce less meat more humanely, without necessarily making


                                      12minutestoclat.com                                        45


protein unaffordable. Many nutritionists argue that high levels of meat consumption in wealthy
countries far exceed dietary needs. The ethical question is not whether humans can eat animals,
but whether they are justified in inflicting large-scale suffering on sentient creatures for the
sake of convenience and low prices, when alternatives exist.
[Extracted with revisions and edits from "Animal Welfare and Industrial Agriculture", The
Humane Society International, and "The Ethics of What We Eat", Peter Singer and Jim
Mason.]

questions.stimulus:
Over the past decade, rates of anxiety, depression, and self-harm among adolescents in many
high-income countries have risen sharply, and the timing has prompted researchers to ask


                                    12minutestoclat.com                                         47


whether the spread of smartphones and social media platforms is partly responsible. Surveys
consistently show that the rise in mental health problems among teenagers coincides closely
with the widespread adoption of social media from around 2012 onwards. Some researchers,
most prominently the social psychologist Jonathan Haidt, argue that this correlation is strong
enough to warrant treating social media as a significant contributing cause.
The proposed mechanisms are plausible. Social media platforms expose adolescents to a
relentless stream of curated images and social comparisons, which can fuel feelings of
inadequacy and low self-worth. The design of these platforms, optimised for engagement
through likes, shares, and notifications, encourages compulsive use that displaces sleep,
exercise, and face-to-face interaction, all of which are known to support mental health. Girls
appear to be more affected than boys, possibly because the image-based and socially
comparative nature of many platforms aligns with the specific insecurities that adolescent girls
are more prone to experiencing.
Other researchers urge caution. The correlations, while consistent, are often statistically
modest, and many studies rely on self-reported data that may not accurately capture either
social media use or mental health status. Crucially, correlation does not establish causation:
teenagers who are already anxious or socially isolated may be heavier users of social media
precisely because they are struggling, rather than struggling because they use social media. The
direction of the relationship remains genuinely contested among researchers.
What is clearer is that the debate should not become a reason for inaction. Even if the causal
evidence is inconclusive, the precautionary case for limiting adolescent social media use is
strengthened by the absence of any demonstrated benefit of heavy use for young people’s
wellbeing. Parents, schools, and regulators need not wait for certainty before taking reasonable
steps to ensure that the environments in which young people grow up are designed with their
long-term interests in mind.
[Extracted with revisions and edits from "The Anxious Generation", Jonathan Haidt, and
"Social Media and Youth Mental Health: The Evidence", Royal Society for Public Health.]
